This paper presents an empirical study showing that "belief states" (essentially, the hidden states of an HMM) are represented linearly in the residual stream of a large language model trained on next token prediction. This study is partially motivated by computational mechanics.

Generally, the reviewers felt that the contribution is solid and the findings are interesting. Some reviewers also expressed enthusiasm for computational mechanics as a potentially useful lens for studying LLMs.

The main reservations were about the simplicity of the setup, the treatment of related work, and the clarity of presentation. On the whole, I'd view the simplicity of the experimental setup as a feature rather than a bug. However, I'm inclined to agree strongly with the later two criticisms. In particular, I think this paper needs to engage substantially with othellogpt and the successor papers. In particular, it's not clear to me what additional information we learn from these experiments beyond what was already known.

Nevertheless, given the overall reviewer enthusiasm, I think it is appropriate to accept the paper and trust the authors to substanstively clarify the relationship and implications for the existing work in this area.
Thank you for the answers. I maintain my initial high score.

Dear Reviewers,

We sincerely thank you all for your reviews on our paper; we believe the paper will be much stronger because of them. We were quite happy by the positive recognition of our work, described as “very important for the interpretability of transformers,” a “fresh perspective,” and “a well executed piece of research.”  While the reviewers were overwhelmingly positive, there was also room for improvements that we take seriously. In particular, we appreciate that all reviewers pointed out a lack of discussion of related work and the applicability of our framework to more complex settings, and reviewer UE1W pointed out important areas to improve on clarity. We take these issues to heart and have responded to them. 

We have added two new analyses and a new subpanel in Fig. 3, see attached PDF.

Due to character limits we were not able to respond as fully as we wanted to. Please ask follow up questions if something is not clear or more detail is needed!

We found two main concerns came up across multiple reviewers, and so will address them here:

**Lack of Discussion of Related Work**

We agree with the reviewers that our submission would be greatly strengthened by connecting it to the existing literature. We will discuss and reference much of the work we brought up in the individual responses with some additions:

* Pal et al (2023) demonstrated that hidden states in LLMs have information about multiple future tokens
* Multiple papers have studied internal representations in transformers, both theoretically (Elhage et al., 2022, Park et al, 2023), and empirically ( Li et al., 2022; Nanda, et al., 2023, Engels et al., 2024).
* In Ortega et. al., (2019), the authors provide a theoretical framework for predictors and agents with persistent memory and trained on nonergodic data, based on a Bayesian framework which builds state machines of sufficient statistics. This is analogous to the MSP which we show transformers learn implicitly despite their apparent lack of persistent memory in the traditional sense. States of the MSP correspond not only to beliefs over the generator states, but also to the minimal sufficient statistics for predicting the future based on the past. One exciting area of further research this exposes is the potential for computational mechanics to inform our understanding of artificial RL agents
* We will also discuss the issue in our response to Reviewer wEQw, section *Issues related to next-token prediction and Chain of Thought (CoT)*, which also touches on the issue of more complex data structures
* Refs to papers about in-context-learning, and discussion similar to *Multiple Belief Simplices* section in response to Reviewer 89Bt.
* There are a number of Computational Mechanics papers which we will discuss that are cited in the individual responses to the reviewers, and in the section immediately following.

**Applicability to More Complex Settings and LLMs**

The framework in this work extends to non-stationary (Riechers and Crutchfield, 2021) and non-ergodic processes (Cruchfield and Marzen, 2015), which is important for the extension to real-world tasks. We limited ourselves to the simpler stationary ergodic setting in this paper to empirically verify important basic features of transformer representations. In the more general setting, we also expect transformers to represent belief-state geometry, although that geometry will then reflect the more general types of non-stationary and non-ergodic processes representative of real-world data like natural language.

With regard to non-HMM data, it is important to note that any dataset made of sequences of tokens used to train a transformer can be represented as being generated from an HMM, if one allows for non-ergodicity, non-stationarity, and infinite states. For example, in the case of training data that takes the form of parenthesis matched strings, one would usually conceive of this as being generated by a push-down automaton. However, this can equivalentaly be represented by an HMM consisting of an infinite chain of hidden states.
Another interesting point that we did not focus on in our presentation for the sake of simplicity, is that even if one does not assume an HMM for the generating machine, the question of the computational structure of an optimal predictor is naturally an HMM, with hidden states given by distinct distributions over the future (whether the generator is an HMM or a Turing Machine, or something else) (Upper, 1997).

With respect to LLMs, we will provide discussion of natural language that are relevant to our framework (Debowski, 2012; Debowski, 2020), which motivates reasoning for why we believe that our framework will apply to that setting, as well as some difficulties. We will also include discussion similar to the Why Fractals section of our response to reviewer exaE, and discuss the Pal et al (2023) results.

Again, we appreciate the work the reviewers have put in here, and are excited to share these results with the world!

Sincerely, 

The Authors

We sincerely thank you for your thoughtful review of our paper. We are particularly grateful for your recognition of our work as offering a "fresh perspective" and presenting a "well-thought-out toy model." Your positive comments on our visualizations are also much appreciated, as we care deeply about the presentation of our work. Additionally, your observation about our work potentially revealing near-optimal rather than perfectly optimal representations has given us food for thought.

We want to clarify an important point regarding your second bullet in Strengths. Our results don't show that the Mess3 HMM or its parameters are directly represented in the residual stream. In particular, we do not show that the parameters of the generative HMM are linearly decodable. Instead, we demonstrate that the belief state geometry associated with the mixed state presentation of the Mess3 HMM is represented. This is the meta-structure an observer of Mess3 emissions would construct to infer the HMM's state, not the HMM structure itself. Despite this nuance, we agree with your assessment that "This is a neat demonstration that a linear projection of the activations of the residual stream aligns well with the ground-truth belief geometry of the Mess3 process."

We address your specific points and questions below.

## Weaknesses

**Why Fractals?**

Thanks for pointing out this opportunity for clarification. Moving beyond stationary ergodic HMM training data, we still generically expect fractal-like structure in the residual-stream activations. Why? The fractal structure is a result of Bayesian updating applied to the “non-deterministic” computational structure of HMMs (Jurgens and Cruchfield, 2021). With stationary processes, this same Bayesian map is folded into itself time and again, producing a very clean fractal. For natural language, even in the absence of stationarity, there will nevertheless be resonances of non-deterministic computational structure, which would imply a type of folding beliefs in a self-similar manner. The more rigorous version of these statements and the empirical validation will be a subject of our future work. We will include a discussion of this in the text upon revision.

**Does this Extend Beyond HMMs?**

We agree that further discussion of this issue is needed. Please see the global response for details on how we plan to address this issue.

We are not exactly sure what a theory-of-mind task is, but are very interested\! Could you provide some more detail or example? This sounds like an interesting thing to think about from the perspective of our framework.

**Residual Stream Contains More Info Than Next Token**

This is an important point to make more clear, as it is central to the conceptual advance of this work. Distinct belief states can have the same next-token distribution. However, distinct belief states are always distinct in their predictions for the entire future, beyond just the next token. Why is this? Intuitively, since belief states are distributions over hidden states of the generative process, and the hidden states of the generative process differ in their distributions over the entire future (but not always in their next-token emissions), the belief states inherent this distinction in future distributions.

Another framing of the MSP states that was not discussed in this paper, but naturally arises in computational mechanics, is that the MSP states are equivalence classes of any-length histories that constrain future sequences in the same way (Upper, 1997). Building up these equivalence classes will give the same MSP structure as the one that arises from the Bayesian updating approach presented in this work. When defined according to these equivalence classes, it is clearly the case that distinct belief states contain information beyond the next token.

As a concrete demonstration of this, we show that transformers represent distinct belief states of the RRXOR process, even though many of these distinct belief states have identical distributions over next tokens.

**Lack of discussion of related work**

We strongly agree that this was lacking in our original submission. Please see the global response for how we plan to address this issue.

## Questions

**What will carry over to other tasks?**

Please see global response for discussion on this issue

**How does recovered geometry change over different points in resid. stream? Is it consistently represented?**

This is a great question. In our analysis of the transformer trained on the RRXOR task we presented evidence that the belief state geometry is not, in general, consistently represented across layers, and is instead represented in a distributed manner across the layers (Fig. 7E, black points). In contrast, for the transformer trained on Mess3 data, we found that the belief state geometry was already well represented by the first layer, and persisted throughout the layers (Fig. 7E, red points). However, as the question implies, there is more work to do in uncovering exactly which situations give rise to this phenomenon, and a more thorough description of the manner in which the belief states are represented. For instance, one question that can be asked in the case of Mess3 is if the representation of the belief state geometry found in Layer 1 is in the same subspace of the residual stream found in the other layers, or if the belief state geometry is similarly represented across context window positions.

A more detailed investigation is beyond the current scope, though we agree these are natural questions to ask, and potentially connect quite directly with open problems in mechanistic interpretability.

## Citations 

Jurgens, AM., and JP. Crutchfield. "Divergent predictive states: The statistical complexity dimension of stationary, ergodic hidden Markov processes." Chaos (2021).

Upper, DR. Theory and algorithms for hidden Markov models and generalized hidden Markov models. UC Berkeley, 1997.

## Weaknesses

We have revised Sec. 2.2 for clarity (see responses to questions below). For issues dealing with simplicity of our experiments and applicability to LLMs, please see global response.

Regarding belief states affecting next token prediction making the results unsurprising: It is true that every belief state has a next-token distribution associated with it. However, in general, multiple belief states have the same next-token distribution. Since transformers are pretrained on next-token prediction it is therefore perhaps not obvious that a transformer should represent distinctions in those belief states, since one might think that if you only care about next-token distributions, there’s no point in distinguishing belief states that have the same next-token distribution. In fact, it is possible to construct the weights of a transformer by hand that perfectly solves the RRXOR task where belief states are NOT linearly represented (Goldstein, 2024).  Our empirical discovery that this representation emerges over pretraining is thus nontrivial.

R2 values in Fig. 7: We will amend the text to be more precise: The belief state geometry (BSG) explains the residual stream geometry beyond the amount that next-token distributions do. A positive correlation between next-token distributions and activations would be a weak test for BSG representation since representations that are not the BSG can also have high amounts of correlation to the next-token distributions.

Because of these concerns, we wanted to directly ask if the BSG explains the geometric structure of activations *beyond* the next token distributions. We compare pairwise distances between residual stream activations to both next-token distributions and ground-truth belief states. For RRXOR, while pairwise distances between next-token distributions weakly correlate with residual stream activations (R2 = 0.31), the correlation with ground-truth belief state distances is much stronger (R2 \= 0.95).

We'll revise line 164: "For the RRXOR process, the correlation with next-token predictions is relatively low (R2 = 0.31), indicating that BSG captures structure in the residual stream not captured by next-token predictions." We'll also update Fig. 7D caption and provide a more detailed explanation of our approach in the text.

## Questions

1. We will fix this  
2. We will add further discussion of prediction vs generation and include references. The task of a generator is to emit sequences of tokens by transitioning between hidden states (Löhr, 2012; Ruebeck et al., 2018). In contrast, the task of a predictor is to predict the future while observing sequences of emissions, without direct access to the hidden states of the generator. Predictors don’t have access to the internal state of the generator, since they are conceived of as being observers of generators. Importantly, a small generative mechanism can be hard to predict. This is a major theme in computational mechanics, which we will give more attention to in our revision.  
3. We will add to line 82 to further clarify the notation and meaning, and update the equation. Upon seeing a belief state η and observing an emission x, the updated belief state η′ is uniquely defined. Thus, the probability associated with that transition is uniquely determined by the previous belief state and the emission, without need to reference the particular belief state one transitions to. We will make this more precise by multiplying the right hand side of the equation by a Kronecker delta function that ensures Equation (1).  
4. We will add the definition: “We label belief states with η_w where w is the shortest string of emissions which leads to that belief state. (In general, an ordering on tokens is required to make this labeling unique.)”  
5. We will add this on line 87: “We refer to the geometric arrangement of the points on the simplex as the belief state geometry.”  
6. We will edit line 49 and Fig. 3 to clarify what the Z1R process is. Please see attached PDF for details.

8. We used before layer norm (LN) as we wanted to study the "internal state" of the transformer. We include new analysis in Fig. R1 in the attached pdf. When we perform the same analyses after the LN our results stay qualitatively the same, and actually become a marginal amount better, in terms of the mean squared error of linearly capturing the belief state geometry.  
9. Degeneracy refers to the fact that the RRXOR MSP contains multiple belief states that have the same distribution over the next token. For clarity, we will amend line 168 to read: “Since the RRXOR process contains distinct belief states with the same optimal next-token distribution, the discovered belief state geometry is not well-explained by the next token predictions.”

## Limitations

Regarding the statement that our work just suggests that the residual streams contain information of HMMs linearly: It is not just that information about the HMM is contained linearly. We provide a much more specific theory and empirical evidence for exactly what information is contained in the residual stream activations, and with what geometric structure. In particular the information contained in the residual stream is the information of the belief states in the mixed-state-presentation, and the geometry is that of the belief state geometry. It is important to note that the representations we find in the transformers are of beliefs over the data-generating HMM states, rather than information about hidden states or the transition probabilities directly. Figure 3 gives an example distinguishing between these different structures.

We are deeply grateful for your insightful review of our paper. Your recognition of our work as "well executed" with "clear writing and ideas" is greatly appreciated. We're particularly pleased that you found our examples and figures helpful in explaining complex concepts like mixed state representation and belief state geometry, as we care deeply about the presentation of our work. We are similarly encouraged by your recognition of our controls.

Your observation that our results have "the flavor of being obvious in hindsight" while acknowledging the importance of actually proving these intuitions is particularly insightful, and we wholeheartedly agree.

We have carefully considered your feedback, including both the strengths you highlighted and the areas for improvement. We address your specific points and questions below, and have additionally performed an extra analysis based on your comments, which you can find in the PDF attached to the global response (Fig. R2):

## Weaknesses

**Will findings generalize to more complex tasks**: We will include a larger discussion about this issue in our revision. Please see the global response for how we plan to address this issue.

**Lack of discussion of related work**: We strongly agree that this was lacking in our original submission. Please see the global response for how we plan to address this issue.

## Questions

These questions are very interesting, and many hit on active areas of research which we plan to address in future work. We don’t have final answers for many of these questions, but for now can give some ideas and interesting perspectives from our framework.

**Multiple Belief Simplices**: The issue of multiple simplices is related to non-ergodic processes, and your intuition for meta-belief states is on the right track. In non-ergodic processes, the data generating HMM consists of multiple disjoint ergodic components. Intuitively, we can think of non-ergodic processes as sets of multiple ergodic HMMs. Data is generated by first choosing one of the ergodic components, and then generating a training example from that HMM. The training data in real LLMs has such non-ergodic structure. For instance, wikipedia articles and personal websites are naturally thought of as being generated by distinct processes. In the case of such non-ergodic processes the MSP describes the joint inference of both determining which ergodic component one is in, and also figuring out which hidden state of the ergodic component one is in. Thus the synchronization process consists of multiple scales of inference. From the perspective of computational mechanics, formal work has shown that this leads to power-law decay in the timescale of synchronization, compared to exponential decay in purely ergodic processes (Crutchfield and Marzen, 2015). Interestingly, this gives a natural explanation for some aspects of in-context learning, such as the empirical finding of power-law decay for loss in context in the largest LLMs (Reid et al., 2024). We are very excited to flesh out this story more formally and connect it to in context learning in future work\!

**Measuring Similarity to Ground Truth, Analysis in High Dimensions, and False Positives**: On the issue of measuring similarity to ground truth and difficulty of high dimensions, we tried to account for these issues with the shuffle, cross-validation controls and by looking at the activations over training. However in the future we plan to devise more methods of validation, and even unsupervised methods to study the represented belief states without knowing ground truth, like PCA. There has been some initial work towards this end, using genetic algorithms over a parametrized family of HMMs (Bowman and Lu, 2024). We are again excited to study and present this in future work\!

**Belief state geometry correlation to task performance**: Regarding how matching the belief state correlates with performance on the task: We've added an analysis to quantify this. Please see Fig. R2 in the attached PDF. Also, In Fig. 6D we show that over training the mean-squared error of the belief state representation decreases. Thus, at least in that example, performance on the task directly correlates with the degree to which the belief states are represented. There has also been research in computational mechanics which describes formally how coarse-graining of the belief state geometry relates to prediction (Marzen and Crutchfield, 2017), which is likely related to the fuzziness of the fractal changing over training, and other work which describes the tradeoff between non-optimal predictive features (analogous to belief states in the MSP) and predictive accuracy (Marzen and Crutchfield, 2016, Marzen et al., 2024).

Marzen, Sarah E., and James P. Crutchfield. "Predictive rate-distortion for infinite-order Markov processes." Journal of Statistical Physics 163 (2016): 1312-1338.

Crutchfield, James P., and Sarah Marzen. "Signatures of infinity: Nonergodicity and resource scaling in prediction, complexity, and learning." Physical Review E 91.5 (2015): 050106.

Thank you for your insightful review of our paper. We appreciate your recognition of our work as "extremely interesting" and "well-verified," as well as your acknowledgment of the paper being "really well-written" with "very insightful" discussion. Your positive remarks about the importance of our observations for transformer interpretability are particularly encouraging.

We're glad you found value in our approach of using mixed-state presentation as a theoretical framework for understanding transformer computations. Your point about the computation being with respect to the input sequence rather than layer-to-layer is indeed a crucial aspect of our work, and we're pleased it resonated with you.

We have carefully considered your feedback, including both the strengths you highlighted and the areas for improvement. We address your specific points below:

## Weaknesses

**Lack of discussion of related work**

We strongly agree that this was lacking in our original submission. Please see the global response for how we plan to address this issue.

**Issues related to next-token prediction and Chain of Thought (CoT)**

We thank the reviewer for bringing up this interesting point, and plan to discuss this issue explicitly in the revised paper. As the reviewer points out, many tasks do not have a structure that, at least intuitively, seems to be naturally captured by next-token prediction dynamics. For instance, tasks may have structures in which many intermediate steps must be considered before arriving at the correct answer, like graph traversing tasks or arithmetic tasks. The structures of these tasks have been both theoretically studied using methods from circuit computational complexity theory (Feng et al., 2024), as well as empirically studied using controlled training data structures (Bachmann et al., 2024). In many of these cases, using seemingly alternative approaches to the traditional token-by-token autoregressive structure, like chain-of-thought, allows transformers to solve these tasks. 

From the perspective of our work, if CoT examples are prevalent during pre-training, then our framework still applies. That is to say, CoT examples are sequential data just like any other, and have a natural interpretation as step-by-step reasoning that gives rise to particular correlation structures between tokens that will be capturable in a particular generating HMM. We therefore expect our framework to apply; a transformer trained on such data will learn the belief state geometry associated with the mixed-state-presentation of that HMM.

The difference between CoT and more traditional approaches exists in the difference between the training data distribution, which will be captured by differently structured generating HMMs, and then reflected in their respective MSPs. We expect that a transformer trained on data containing a mix of CoT and non-CoT examples for the same problems, will implement a mixed-state-presentation that contains structures related to each. An exciting research project that we intend to pursue in the future is to study the types of MSPs and belief state geometry structures induced by CoT vs non-CoT training data, and then use this to explain why and how CoT helps transformers perform more complicated tasks.

Here we have focused on simpler training data structure in order to present and experimentally verify the overall framework and its applicability to pretrained transformers. We are very excited to study the geometric structures induced by particular types of data (like chain-of-thought) or training paradigms (like RL methods after pretraining) from the perspective of our framework in future work.

## Questions
1. **Context length interaction with optimal prediction**: This is an important point to clarify. In our experiments transformers are trained in the normal way, such that a particular context window position only has access to positions within the context position earlier to it (and itself). So for example, in our experiments with a context window of length 10, position 5 in the context window only gets input from 5 tokens. The MSP maps onto this setup quite naturally, as it describes the process of updating beliefs as one observes more and more tokens, starting from no observations. In the MSP, there are transient belief states that arise from the fewer number of observations, which are distinct from the belief states accessible after observation of a full context window.

2. **Why does MSP for RRXOR have finite states?**:  Yes, there is a quick explanation for the finite states in the RRXOR MSP which has an interesting general lesson, having to do with a property of HMMs called unifilarity. An HMM is unifilar if given a current hidden state and a particular emission, there is at most one next-state to go to (i.e. the conditional distribution of the next state given the current state and an emission is deterministic). Interestingly, the recurrent component of the MSP will always be the minimal unifilar HMM that produces its data. The RRXOR HMM is minimal and unifilar, and so we know that the recurrent component of its MSP will have a finite set of states, in this case 5 states. Thus, once enough data is seen such that one is synchronized to the generating HMM, we are assured to be in a recurrent component with 5 states (in this case 5). Showing that there are a finite number of transient belief states is less obvious, but can be worked out for each particular case. In contrast to the RRXOR process, the Mess3 HMM is not unifilar and has infinitely many belief states. Data-generating HMMs that are not unifilar generically have infinite-state MSPs.

Bachmann, G., and V, Nagarajan. "The pitfalls of next-token prediction." arXiv  (2024).

Feng, Guhao, et al. "Towards revealing the mystery behind chain of thought: a theoretical perspective." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (2024).

summary.value: This paper proposes that the mixed-state presentation that is grounded in optimal prediction can explain the representations and computational steps in transformers over a sequence generated by some simple hidden Markov chains. This is done by first training the transformer until convergence, and then fitting a linear regression from residual stream activations to the optimal belief state. The authors observe that this procedure mimics the theoretical prediction from mixed-state presentations and reveals similar fractal patterns. Here, what is remarkable is that there is only a single linear transformation between hidden representations of the transformer and the optimal belief state geometry. The authors also reveal that for some tasks with degeneracy, residual streams across layers need to be concatenated to have the same observation.

strengths.value:
1. The paper presents an extremely interesting empirical observation on the hidden activations of transformer architecture. The results seem to be well-verified. The fact that the optimal belief-state geometry appears gradually is also very interesting.

2. This empirical observation points to a mixed-state presentation as the theoretical framework for how to think about transformer computations. Crucially, here, the computation is with respect to the input sequence rather than layer to layer. This is very important for the interpretability of transformers. The authors also note the possibility of generalizing the observations in the paper to other architectures, which would be interesting to see.

3. Overall, paper is really well-written and the discussion is very insightful.

weaknesses.value:
1. The paper has no discussion of the related work. I like the directness of the presentation, but there must be some prior or related literature? I am adding two papers that I thought were relevant to the discussion in the paper:

Bachmann, Gregor, and Vaishnavh Nagarajan. "The pitfalls of next-token prediction." arXiv preprint arXiv:2403.06963 (2024).
Hu, Jiachen, Qinghua Liu, and Chi Jin. "On Limitation of Transformer for Learning HMMs." arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.04089 (2024).


2. The claims on next-token prediction L216-224 are not necessarily realized for many tasks and settings, which forces many authors to devise other schemes to train (e.g., chain-of-thought). This might be a problem that comes with the fact that one cannot minimize harder problems than the ones considered in this paper due to difficulties in optimization or the sample complexities needed, which are not at all discussed in the paper. Related to the previous point above, these should be discussed more thoroughly.

3. The findings are limited to simple problems; transformers are trained until convergence, which has very good generalization capabilities, but I think the paper has a lot of interesting insights already.

summary.value: The paper studies the geometric structure of how belief states are represented in the residual stream of transformers using relevant theory from computational mechanics. The main object of investigation of the paper is a transformer model trained on data generated using an HMM. Following this, the theory of optimal prediction is used to make predictions about the possible geometry of belief states in the residual stream. The results report that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream and contain information about the future beyond the next token prediction.

strengths.value:
- Fresh perspective and well-thought-out toy model: The paper introduces a way to look at learned representations from the perspective of computational mechanics by studying the geometric structure of the belief states for a toy model trained on the task of language modeling on data from an HMM. The control exercised by the toy model allows for having a notion of the expected optimal structure as given by the optimal predictor on the task. 
- The geometric structure of the activations in the residual stream implies that the model accurately recovers the parameters of the HMM and that the parameters of the HMM are linearly decodable from the activations. This is a neat demonstration that a linear projection of the activations of the residual stream aligns well with the ground-truth belief geometry of the Mess3 process.
- The visualizations are well made.

weaknesses.value:
- There is little to no discussion or intuition provided on what it would mean for the belief state geometry to have a "fractal structure"? Is it a domain-specific expectation to have given the data distribution structure imposed by the HMM? 
- It is unclear how the finding holds beyond data distributions generated using an HMM. How does the representation of the belief structure change for real-world / theory-of-mind tasks? How would one measure it? 
- It is unclear how the implicature "the residual stream contains information about the future beyond just the next token" is made.  
- There is no discussion of related work in the introduction and the paper, making it a bit difficult to situate this work and compare its findings in the context of other related papers.

questions.value:
- What aspects of the findings from the paper will carry over to real tasks?
- How does the recovered geometry change over different points in the residual stream? Are the belief states consistently linearly represented?

limitations.value:
The discussion of the limitations of the work is well done. I especially like the point the authors make about "Computational Mechanics is primarily concerned with optimal prediction, but LLMs in practice are not perfectly optimal. Further work is needed to understand how near-optimality and non-optimality influence belief state representations."

Even in the context of the toy model trained on data from the HMM the ground-truth fractal structure is not "perfectly" recovered. This perhaps hints at the model learning a near-optimal representation, rather than the optimal representation. Nonetheless, very interesting!

summary.value: The authors present evidence that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformer-based large language models. They also argue that belief state geometry represents information beyond next-token prediction and can be spread across the residual streams of multiple layers. This work contributes to understanding the ability of the transformer structure.

strengths.value:
- Their results show that only next-token predictions with the transformer structure can represent belief states. This is an important empirical contribution to the interpretability field.
- The authors provide nice visualizations, such as the figure for the fractal geometry.

weaknesses.value:
- The formalization in Section 2.2 is very ambiguous. See the Questions below.
- More experiments are needed for a larger number of hidden states and vocab sizes.
- It is only for the HMM model, not language models.
- The belief state $\eta$ directly affects the next word prediction, so it may be very natural. Not that surprising. As they mentioned, it might be because the models use a residual stream and were pre-trained on next-token prediction.
- Even if $R^2=0.31$ in Figure 7, there is a positive correlation. I don’t understand why they said RRXOR belief state geometry is not captured by next-token predictions alone. If so, what else is the geometry captured by?

questions.value:
- In Figure 2, $T^{(1)}$ seems wrong.
- In line 63, you said, “Computational mechanics shows that prediction is substantially more complicated than generation.” What’s the difference between prediction and generation? Does “prediction” mean the inference for the hidden state given the observations? Also, even if “computational mechanics” is a large field, you need to provide some reference for such arguments.
- In Equation (1), $\eta’$ is like $\mathrm{Pr}(s_i \mid x, \eta)$ based on Bayes' rule. The notation is a little ambiguous. Especially, in line 82, what does $\mathrm{Pr}(\eta’ , x\mid \eta)$ mean? There is no $\eta’$ in the RHS. Does it mean that the probability is the same for all $\eta’$?
- In line 90,  $\eta_{10}$ and $\eta_{01}$ are not defined. Maybe you should define $\eta_{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_N}$.
- I think you defined the belief state as a probability distribution $\eta$. Then, what is the definition of belief state geometry?
- What is Z1R in Figure 3?
- In Figure 3C, how do we read each point? What’s the meaning of the point $\eta_{10}$? Does this mean, 50% for $S_0$, 50% for $S_1$, and 50% for $S_R$? I think you need to draw three axes for each one to present the probability simplex.
- In line 122, why did you use the residual stream before the layer norm?
- In line 168, what do you mean by “degeneracies”?

limitations.value: As they mentioned, there is no extension to LLMs. This work just suggests that the residual streams contain the information of HMMs linearly.

summary.value: This work uses a new theoretical framework from Computational Mechanics to analyze representations in transformers. Using these tools, the authors can convert between a data-generating structure, such as one modeled with a Hidden Markov Model, and a geometric structure in a probability simplex that describes the beliefs over the states of the data-generating structure given finite observations. They then use linear readout analysis to see if the geometric structure can be linearly decoded from transformer representations and find that, indeed, they can. Thus, the authors discover that transformers represent more than just the structure of the data generating process; they also represent the current belief of the state of this process. The authors reason that this is ultimately advantageous for next-token prediction, because a model that can more accurately infer the current hidden state will be able to better predict future tokens, if not the immediately next one: “even if different belief states imply the same probability distribution over the next token, any distinction in probability distributions over the entire future may eventually, after further context, imply distinct distributions over the next token at some point in the future”.

strengths.value:
This is a well executed piece of research. The writing and ideas are clear; as someone without any background in computational mechanics, there are adequate examples and figures to walk through the ideas, explaining concepts such as the mixed state representation and belief state geometry. 

Also appreciated are the high level intuitions, such as the discussion on prediction vs generation, which helps to anchor the goal of pursuing the belief simplex in transformers  (e.g., “Computational Mechanics shows that prediction is substantially more complicated than generation. Informally, the reason for this is that even if one knows the underlying hidden generative structure, one must still perform computational work in order to infer which state the generative process is in given finite observations of data.”), and the discussion on why it might be useful for a model to discover these representations (e.g., “for a recurrent neural network to perform as well as possible on next token prediction, all information about the past necessary to predict the entire future as well as possible must be present in the latent state of the network.“). 

While it might be easy to cast the results as obvious, they have the flavor of being obvious *in hindsight*; that transformers form these kinds of representations certainly makes a lot of sense, but the work still needs to be done to analyze that this is indeed the case, and the authors here do a great job proving it.

The experiments are simple, but completely adequate. The standout is figure 6, which includes a number of careful controls which show that: the belief-state geometry emerges throughout training; the regression task withstands held-out validation; and the regression mapping can be collapsed if the input-output pairings are shuffled, demonstrating that the geometry is not spurious.

I cannot be certain of this work’s originality as I’m not an expert in the field of interpretability, but I have not encountered any papers that do a similar analysis.

weaknesses.value:
One weakness might be that it will be difficult to demonstrate similar findings in more complex tasks, especially those for which we do not have ground truth data-generating models. This could limit the significance of the findings and the usefulness of the techniques, since they would only be applicable to toy domains. I do not think this needs to be addressed in this work necessarily, and the authors do point out as much towards the end of the paper.

While I do not think a full “related work” section is needed, a few more references to past work and similar types of analyses would have been appreciated to compare and contrast the findings and techniques, and to serve as a starting point for those who wish to dive deeper into the literature.

questions.value:
Can a network represent multiple belief simplexes (simplices?), and if so, how fluidly might it switch between them? If, up to the current token, the “correct” data structure is still ambiguous, would the transformer represent a meta-belief state over the possible structures?

How can one measure similarity to the ground truth more quantitatively?

How hard is this analysis to perform in higher data-structure dimensions?

How much does one need to worry about false positives?

How might the analysis go wrong, or be misleading?

How does matching of the ground truth belief state correlate with performance on the task?

title.value: Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry in their Residual Stream

abstract.value: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Here, we present evidence that this structure is given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data- generating process. Leveraging the theory of optimal prediction, we anticipate and then find that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformers, even in cases where the predicted belief state geometry has highly nontrivial fractal structure. We investigate cases where the belief state geometry is represented in the final residual stream or distributed across the residual streams of multiple layers, providing a framework to explain these observations. Furthermore we demonstrate that the inferred belief states contain information about the entire future, beyond the local next-token prediction that the transformers are explicitly trained on. Our work provides a general framework connecting the structure of training data to the geometric structure of activations inside transformers.

TLDR.value: Transformers trained on next-token prediction learn to represent the geometry of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process in their residual stream.

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
